title: Ang 1020–1033: Nanak's Solhe
tomorrow: what was there before there was anything at all?

cards: Subtitles or dubbed? People fight about it over every foreign show. One side says you lose the actor's real voice.
The other says you can't follow a story you can't understand. Sikh families have a version of that argument about the Guru's words, and today's pages make it sharp.
They hold Guru Nanak's Solhe, long hymns that run on and on, with a rhythm you can feel even before you know what a single word means.

teach.b: Solhe is read as sixteens: hymns built of sixteen stanzas, here in Guru Nanak's voice, praising the One who made everything and holds it in order.
Read one aloud and the length becomes a kind of music, stanza after stanza, the same pulse coming back. Now the argument.

One view says: hear it in Gurmukhi. The sounds, the rhymes, the exact words the Guru chose are part of the hymn, and no translation carries all of it. A translation is a window; the original is the room.
That's why some families learn to read Gurmukhi even when they speak English at home. The other view says: the point is to understand.
People on this side note that the Gurus sang in the everyday speech of the people listening, not in a language only scholars knew.
So if the listener now thinks in English, give them the meaning, or the words just wash past. Both sides want the same thing, for the hymn to land.
One guards the sound, the other guards the sense.
And some sangats do both: the Gurmukhi sung, and a translation shown beside it.

how: Guru Nanak's Maru Solhe are sung in kirtan and read in a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; they are read in Gurmukhi, and some sangats show a translation alongside.

o: a ballad of steps, each one a stanza
long hymns built of sixteen stanzas
short two-line verses sung in the evening

a window, not the whole room

s: Sikhs all agree a translation of Gurbani is just as good as the original
one view guards the Gurmukhi sound; the other guards the sense. some sangats keep both.
the Solhe are long hymns built of sixteen stanzas
people who want translations don't care about Gurmukhi
they want the same thing, for the hymn to land, and note the Gurus sang in everyday speech.

games.q: your friend says reading Gurbani only in English is fine. you love the Gurmukhi. what's the strongest case for her side?
o: the Gurus sang in their listeners' everyday speech; meaning is the point.
Gurmukhi is too hard now, so nobody needs to bother learning it.
a newer translation is more modern, so it must be closer to the truth.
games.why: her best case is the hymn's own aim: to be understood. your best case is that the sound carries the Guru's exact words. both want it to land.

practice: Say one line you know in another language out loud, slowly, a line of Gurbani if you have one, or any line from a song or a grandparent. Then say what it means in your own words. Sit with whichever version stays with you.
